text:
Every recursive resolver keeps answers it has already received. Each DNS record carries a TTL (time to live), a 32-bit counter of seconds defined in RFC 1035. The TTL lets the resolver reuse an answer without asking the authoritative server again.

This causes delays when records change. Say you change an A record at noon, and its TTL is 3600 seconds. A resolver that fetched the old record at 11:59 will keep serving the old IP address until almost 1 p.m. Clients assume that address is current, because nothing tells them otherwise. So the time it takes a change to spread (propagation) depends on when cached copies expire, not on when you made the edit.

Failed lookups are cached too. Suppose a resolver cached an NXDOMAIN ("no such name") answer before your new subdomain existed. Under RFC 2308 negative caching, it will keep saying the subdomain doesn't exist until the SOA minimum time runs out.

Browsers and operating system stub resolvers add their own private caches on top. Some of them ignore TTLs entirely.

Call this "TTL debt." To avoid it, operators should plan migrations in two steps. First, lower the TTL to 300 seconds, doing so one full old-TTL period before the migration. Then migrate. Otherwise, the internet keeps navigating by an outdated map.
